Reference: Card et al. (2015)

Model Setting

The paper asks when a regression kink design (RKD) identifies an interpretable causal effect of a continuous policy variable that is a known, deterministic but kinked function of an endogenous assignment variable. The motivating example is unemployment insurance (UI): benefits are a fixed fraction of previous earnings up to a maximum, so conditional on earnings there is no variation in benefits, and any candidate instrument independent of earnings is also independent of benefits. The idea is to look for a kink in the relationship between the assignment variable and the outcome that coincides with the kink in the policy rule, and to divide the change in the outcome slope by the change in the policy slope. Earlier work (Nielsen, Sorensen and Taber 2010) justified this ratio only in a constant-effect additive model. The paper establishes identification in a general nonseparable model with unrestricted heterogeneity, under two key conditions: the density of the assignment variable conditional on the unobservables is continuously differentiable at the kink (smooth density), and the policy rule is continuous at the kink. It then delivers four results. First, the sharp RKD estimand equals the treatment-on-the-treated (TT) parameter of Florens, Heckman, Meghir and Vytlacil (2008), equivalently the local average response of Altonji and Matzkin (2005), which is a weighted average of marginal effects over the whole population with weights proportional to each type's relative likelihood of being at the kink. Second, a fuzzy RKD that allows for unobserved determinants of the policy, noncompliance and measurement error in both the assignment and the policy variable identifies, under a monotonicity condition, a weighted average of marginal effects whose weights also scale with each type's own kink and with the probability that the assignment variable is measured without error. Third, the smoothness conditions imply testable restrictions: the density of the assignment variable and the conditional distribution of predetermined covariates must have no kink at the threshold.

Fourth, the paper reviews local polynomial estimation and the robust bias-corrected inference of Calonico, Cattaneo and Titiunik (2014) (CCT), proposes fuzzy analogs of the CCT and Imbens and Kalyanaraman (2012) (IK) bandwidths, and applies a fuzzy RKD to the kink in the Austrian UI benefit schedule at the maximum benefit, using about 275,000 claims from 2001 to 2012. The density of base-year earnings shows no kink at the threshold (t-statistic 1.61 for the change in slope). Local linear estimates with the larger bandwidths chosen by the fuzzy CCT, fuzzy IK and Fan and Gijbels (FG) selectors give elasticities of unemployment duration with respect to benefits between 1.4 and 1.9, but the CCT robust confidence intervals are wide, only one of these three is significant, and local quadratic estimates are too noisy to be informative.

Environment and Target Parameter

The outcome is generated by the generalized nonseparable model:

Y=y(B,V,U)(1)Y=y(B,V,U) \tag{1}Y=y(B,V,U)(1)

where YYY is the outcome, BBB is a continuous regressor of interest (the policy variable), VVV is an observed covariate (the assignment or running variable), and UUU is a potentially multidimensional error that enters yyy nonadditively. This is a special case of Imbens and Newey (2009) with two observable covariates. When BBB is binary the individual treatment effect is y(1,V,U)−y(0,V,U)y(1,V,U)-y(0,V,U)y(1,V,U)−y(0,V,U), and when BBB is continuous it is ∂y(b,V,U)/∂b\partial y(b,V,U)/\partial b∂y(b,V,U)/∂b. With discrete outcomes or durations, YYY can be read as an individual-specific probability or expected value, and the results apply to the observed outcome because its conditional expectations coincide with those of YYY. For a continuous regressor, Florens et al. (2008) define the treatment-on-the-treated parameter:

TTb∣v(b,v)=∫∂y(b,v,u)∂bdFU∣B=b,V=v(u)(2)TT_{b|v}(b,v)=\int\frac{\partial y(b,v,u)}{\partial b}dF_{U|B=b,V=v}(u) \tag{2}TTb∣v​(b,v)=∫∂b∂y(b,v,u)​dFU∣B=b,V=v​(u)(2)

which is the average effect of a marginal increase in bbb at a specific pair (b,v)(b,v)(b,v), holding fixed the distribution of unobservables FU∣B=b,V=v(⋅)F_{U|B=b,V=v}(\cdot)FU∣B=b,V=v​(⋅) of the units actually at that pair. In the UI example, YYY is expected unemployment duration, BBB the benefit level and VVV pre-job-loss earnings, and the policy rule is:

B=b(V)=ρmin⁡(V,T)(3)B=b(V)=\rho\min(V,T) \tag{3}B=b(V)=ρmin(V,T)(3)

with replacement rate ρ\rhoρ and threshold TTT. Since BBB is a deterministic function of VVV, the model is not nonparametrically identified by conventional instruments, but a causal effect of BBB on YYY should induce a kink in E[Y∣V=v]E[Y|V=v]E[Y∣V=v] at v=Tv=Tv=T. The threshold is normalized to T=0T=0T=0 from here on.

Nielsen, Sorensen and Taber (2010) analyze the constant-effect additive model:

Y=τB+g(V)+ε(4)Y=\tau B+g(V)+\varepsilon \tag{4}Y=τB+g(V)+ε(4)

with B=b(V)B=b(V)B=b(V) continuous and kinked at V=0V=0V=0. If g(⋅)g(\cdot)g(⋅) and E[ε∣V=v]E[\varepsilon|V=v]E[ε∣V=v] have derivatives that are continuous in vvv at v=0v=0v=0, then the RKD estimand recovers τ\tauτ:

τ=lim⁡v0→0+dE[Y∣V=v]dv∣v=v0−lim⁡v0→0−dE[Y∣V=v]dv∣v=v0lim⁡v0→0+b′(v0)−lim⁡v0→0−b′(v0)(5)\tau=\frac{\lim_{v_0\to0^+}\left.\frac{dE[Y|V=v]}{dv}\right|_{v=v_0}-\lim_{v_0\to0^-}\left.\frac{dE[Y|V=v]}{dv}\right|_{v=v_0}}{\lim_{v_0\to0^+}b'(v_0)-\lim_{v_0\to0^-}b'(v_0)} \tag{5}τ=limv0​→0+​b′(v0​)−limv0​→0−​b′(v0​)limv0​→0+​dvdE[Y∣V=v]​​v=v0​​−limv0​→0−​dvdE[Y∣V=v]​​v=v0​​​(5)

that is, the change in slope of the conditional expectation function at the kink divided by the change in slope of the assignment rule. A proportional hazards model for durations with a constant benefit coefficient and multiplicative unobserved heterogeneity (as in Meyer 1990) does not fit this additive form, but it is a special case of the nonseparable model, which also lets the heterogeneity be correlated with VVV and BBB.

Sharp RKD: Assumptions

Let (V,U)(V,U)(V,U) be a pair of random variables, with VVV one-dimensional and observed and UUU unobserved of arbitrary dimension. Let IVI_VIV​ be an arbitrarily small closed interval around 000, Ib(V)I_{b(V)}Ib(V)​ its image under bbb, and IS1,…,SkI_{S_1,\ldots,S_k}IS1​,…,Sk​​ the product of the supports of S1,…,SkS_1,\ldots,S_kS1​,…,Sk​. The sharp RK design rests on four assumptions:

  • Assumption 1 (regularity): the support of UUU is a subset of an arbitrarily large compact set IU⊂RmI_U\subset\mathbb{R}^mIU​⊂Rm; yyy is continuous and partially differentiable in its first two arguments, and y1(b,v,u)y_1(b,v,u)y1​(b,v,u) is continuous on Ib(V),V,UI_{b(V),V,U}Ib(V),V,U​. Bounded support can be replaced by dominance of y1y_1y1​ by an integrable function, which is all that is needed to interchange differentiation and integration.

  • Assumption 2 (smooth effect of VVV): y2(b,v,u)y_2(b,v,u)y2​(b,v,u) is continuous on Ib(V),V,UI_{b(V),V,U}Ib(V),V,U​. This is much weaker than an exclusion restriction: VVV may affect YYY directly as long as its marginal effect is continuous.

  • Assumption 3 (first stage and nonnegligible population at the kink): b(⋅)b(\cdot)b(⋅) is known, everywhere continuous and continuously differentiable on IV∖{0}I_V\setminus\{0\}IV​∖{0}, with lim⁡v→0+b′(v)≠lim⁡v→0−b′(v)\lim_{v\to0^+}b'(v)\neq\lim_{v\to0^-}b'(v)limv→0+​b′(v)=limv→0−​b′(v); and the set AU={u:fV∣U=u(v)>0 ∀v∈IV}A_U=\{u:f_{V|U=u}(v)>0\ \forall v\in I_V\}AU​={u:fV∣U=u​(v)>0 ∀v∈IV​} has positive measure, ∫AUdFU(u)>0\int_{A_U}dF_U(u)>0∫AU​​dFU​(u)>0. Continuity of bbb rules out a simultaneous jump in the level of the policy.

  • Assumption 4 (smooth density): fV∣U=u(v)f_{V|U=u}(v)fV∣U=u​(v) and ∂fV∣U=u(v)/∂v\partial f_{V|U=u}(v)/\partial v∂fV∣U=u​(v)/∂v are continuous on IV,UI_{V,U}IV,U​.

Assumption 4 is the key identifying condition. Continuity of fV∣U=uf_{V|U=u}fV∣U=u​ is enough for a regression discontinuity design but not for a kink design, which needs continuity of its derivative. The condition rules out deterministic sorting, in which agents precisely choose VVV (such as the bunching at kinks predicted by frictionless models, Saez 2010), but it allows VVV to be correlated with UUU and allows agents to influence VVV with optimization errors (Chetty 2012).

Fuzzy RKD: Setup and Assumptions

In practice the observed policy deviates from the formula because the formula depends on other unobserved variables, because of noncompliance, or because of measurement error. The fuzzy design writes B=b(V,ε)B=b(V,\varepsilon)B=b(V,ε), where the vector ε\varepsilonε (possibly correlated with UUU) captures unobserved inputs and compliance types. In the UI illustration, ε=(ε1,ε2)\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2)ε=(ε1​,ε2​), where the binary ε1\varepsilon_1ε1​ indicates dependents (benefit schedules b1(v)b_1(v)b1​(v) with and b0(v)b_0(v)b0​(v) without dependents) and ε2\varepsilon_2ε2​ indicates whether a claimant is an always taker (claims b1(v)b_1(v)b1​(v)), never taker (claims b0(v)b_0(v)b0​(v)), complier (claims bε1(v)b_{\varepsilon_1}(v)bε1​​(v)) or defier (claims b1−ε1(v)b_{1-\varepsilon_1}(v)b1−ε1​​(v)). Apart from bounded support, the distribution of ε\varepsilonε is unrestricted, and FU,εF_{U,\varepsilon}FU,ε​ denotes the joint measure of UUU and ε\varepsilonε. The observed values V∗V^*V∗ and B∗B^*B∗ contain measurement error:

The fuzzy design replaces Assumptions 1, 3 and 4 and adds two more:

Assumption 3a requires a nonnegligible group that simultaneously has a nontrivial individual kink, has UV=0U_V=0UV​=0 and has positive density near the threshold. The mass point of UVU_VUV​ at zero is critical: without it the first-stage kink is smoothed away, as in a fuzzy RD with continuous measurement error, and further assumptions on the error would be needed. No mass point is needed for UBU_BUB​. In the Austrian data most observations lie exactly on the benefit schedule, which the authors read as a mass point at zero in (UV,UB)(U_V,U_B)(UV​,UB​). Assumption 4a lets VVV, UV′U_{V'}UV′​ and UB′U_{B'}UB′​ be arbitrarily correlated, and Assumption 5 lets the mass point probabilities depend on everything as long as they are smooth in VVV. Assumption 6 is the analog of the Imbens and Angrist (1994) monotonicity condition: no one's kink goes in the opposite direction. It holds in the UI application because the benefit schedules for different numbers of dependents are parallel.

Testable Implications

The smoothness conditions deliver two testable predictions. Corollary 1: in a valid sharp RKD, fV(v)f_V(v)fV​(v) is continuously differentiable in vvv; in a valid fuzzy RKD, fV∗(v∗)f_{V^*}(v^*)fV∗​(v∗) is continuously differentiable in v∗v^*v∗. In the sharp case this follows from integrating the smooth conditional densities over types:

fV(v)=∫fV∣U=u(v)dFU(u)(22)f_V(v)=\int f_{V|U=u}(v)dF_U(u) \tag{22}fV​(v)=∫fV∣U=u​(v)dFU​(u)(22)

A kink or a jump in the density of the assignment variable at the threshold signals deterministic sorting, in the spirit of the McCrary (2008) manipulation test for RD designs. In the fuzzy case, both Assumption 4a and Assumption 5 are needed for fV∗f_{V^*}fV∗​ to be smooth, so a kink or jump in fV∗f_{V^*}fV∗​ means that at least one fails. For the second prediction, Assumption 7 posits predetermined covariates X=x(U)X=x(U)X=x(U) in the sharp design and X=x(U,ε)X=x(U,\varepsilon)X=x(U,ε) in the fuzzy design, determined before VVV (so XXX excludes VVV and BBB). Corollary 2: under Assumption 7, in a valid sharp RKD dPr⁡[X≤x∣V=v]/dvd\Pr[X\leq x|V=v]/dvdPr[X≤x∣V=v]/dv is continuous at v=0v=0v=0 for all xxx, and in a valid fuzzy RKD dPr⁡[X≤x∣V∗=v∗]/dv∗d\Pr[X\leq x|V^*=v^*]/dv^*dPr[X≤x∣V∗=v∗]/dv∗ is continuous at v∗=0v^*=0v∗=0 for all xxx. In the sharp case:

Pr⁡[X≤x∣V=v]=∫1[x(u)≤x]fV∣U=u(v)fV(v)dFU(u)(23)\Pr[X\leq x|V=v]=\int1\left[x(u)\leq x\right]\frac{f_{V|U=u}(v)}{f_V(v)}dF_U(u) \tag{23}Pr[X≤x∣V=v]=∫1[x(u)≤x]fV​(v)fV∣U=u​(v)​dFU​(u)(23)

which inherits the continuous differentiability of the type weights. This test checks Assumption 4 (or Assumptions 4a and 5 jointly) the way baseline balance tests check randomization, and parallels the covariate continuity test of Lee (2008) for RD designs, but the RKD implication is stronger: the derivatives of the conditional expectations or quantiles of XXX with respect to VVV must be continuous at the kink, not only their levels.

and the fuzzy RKD estimator is the ratio of the reduced-form to the first-stage kink, the kink analog of the fuzzy RD (Wald) estimator:

where ϱ\varrhoϱ and Ω\OmegaΩ are the asymptotic bias and variance. The rate nh3\sqrt{nh^3}nh3​, slower than the nh\sqrt{nh}nh​ of RD, reflects that a derivative rather than a level is estimated at the boundary. Although identification implies that E[Y∣V=v]E[Y|V=v]E[Y∣V=v] is continuous at the threshold, with a uniform kernel imposing continuity in estimation changes neither the asymptotic variance (Card, Lee, Pei and Weber 2012) nor the asymptotic bias.

Three implementation choices follow. For the polynomial order, the logic by which Hahn, Todd and van der Klaauw (2001) prefer local linear to local constant regression in RD (bias of order h2h^2h2 rather than hhh) would favor local quadratic for boundary derivatives, but rate arguments alone cannot justify a universal choice: the MSE-best order depends on the sample size and on the derivatives of E[Y∣V=v]E[Y|V=v]E[Y∣V=v] and E[B∣V=v]E[B|V=v]E[B∣V=v] in the data, and the authors suggest choosing ppp by simulations from DGPs that mimic the data or by comparing estimated asymptotic MSEs. For the kernel, a uniform kernel is used, with similar results from the boundary-optimal triangular kernel. For the bandwidth, the IK MSE-optimal RD bandwidth and the CCT bandwidth for a jump in the ν\nuν-th derivative (ν=1\nu=1ν=1 for RKD) are extended in two ways. First, both selectors contain a regularization term that guards against large bandwidths; its RK version yields bandwidths that are too small in this application, and since dropping it does not change the asymptotic properties, unregularized versions are also used. Second, the default CCT bandwidth is MSE-optimal for the reduced-form kink, not for τ^FRKD\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{FRKD}}τ^FRKD​, so the paper derives fuzzy CCT and fuzzy IK bandwidths optimal for the ratio (Supplemental Material, Section B.2), along with the rule-of-thumb FG bandwidth.

Because the MSE-optimal bandwidth leaves a nonvanishing bias, conventional intervals can undercover. CCT estimate the bias ϱp\varrho_pϱp​ by a local polynomial of order q≥p+1q\geq p+1q≥p+1 with pilot bandwidth hqh_qhq​, compute the variance varpbc\mathrm{var}^{bc}_pvarpbc​ of the bias-corrected estimator accounting for the sampling variation of both terms, and form the robust 95 percent interval:

τ^pbc≡τ^p−hpϱ^p,τ^pbc±1.96varpbc(29)\hat{\tau}^{bc}_p\equiv\hat{\tau}_p-h^p\hat{\varrho}_p,\qquad\hat{\tau}^{bc}_p\pm1.96\sqrt{\mathrm{var}^{bc}_p} \tag{29}τ^pbc​≡τ^p​−hpϱ^​p​,τ^pbc​±1.96varpbc​​(29)

which requires hq/h→ρ∈(0,∞)h_q/h\to\rho\in(0,\infty)hq​/h→ρ∈(0,∞) as n→∞n\to\inftyn→∞. Ganong and Jaeger (2014) raise concerns about RKD estimates when the outcome is highly nonlinear in the running variable and propose a permutation test, which the authors apply in the companion working paper. When (B,V)(B,V)(B,V) and (Y,V)(Y,V)(Y,V) come from different data sets, a two-sample version applies (Supplemental Material, Section B.1).

Application: Austrian UI Benefits and Data

The application estimates the effect of UI benefits on unemployment duration, the moral hazard side of the Baily (1978) trade-off between search incentives and risk sharing. Job losers in Austria who worked at least 52 weeks in the past 24 months are eligible. The daily benefit is 55 percent of net daily earnings in the base year, subject to a maximum adjusted annually, which creates a piecewise linear schedule in base-year earnings (net of Social Security and income tax) with a kink where the maximum binds. Claimants with dependents receive supplements by number of dependents, which are added to the base benefit and not capped. Because dependents are unobserved, they are treated as an unobserved determinant of benefits in a fuzzy RKD, and monotonicity holds because the schedules for different numbers of dependents are parallel.

The data come from the Austrian Social Security Database (ASSD), which records daily employment and unemployment spells and annual earnings by employer (up to the contribution cap) for all private sector workers, merged with UI claim records (claim date, daily benefit received, duration of registered unemployment). Base-year earnings, assigned from claim dates, are the observed assignment variable V∗V^*V∗, and the outcome is the duration of registered unemployment, censored at one year. The sample covers claims from 2001 to 2012 by claimants with at least one year of tenure who claimed within four weeks of job loss (excluding quitters, who face a four-week waiting period), excluding those with zero base-year earnings, those older than 50, those above the Social Security earnings cap and those low enough to face other nonlinearities in the schedule. Years are pooled by centering earnings at each year's threshold for the maximum benefit, giving about 275,000 observations.

Application: Validity Checks and Graphical Evidence

  • Density: the histogram of base-year earnings in 300-euro bins (about 4,200 observations per bin) declines smoothly through the threshold. Polynomial models fitted by minimum chi-squared, imposing continuity but letting the first and higher derivatives change at the threshold, select a fourth-order polynomial by the Akaike criterion (goodness of fit 75.6, p-value 0.05). The estimated change in the first derivative of the density is 2.00×10−42.00\times10^{-4}2.00×10−4 with standard error 1.24×10−41.24\times10^{-4}1.24×10−4, a t-statistic of 1.61, so the smooth density prediction of Corollary 1 is not rejected.

  • First stage: average daily benefits rise roughly linearly from about 29 to about 39 euros over the 14,000 euros of earnings below the threshold and flatten sharply above it; the residual positive slope above the threshold reflects family allowances, whose average number rises with earnings.

  • Reduced form: mean unemployment duration rises from about 100 days to about 118 days below the threshold and flattens above it, a visible but noisier kink.

Application: Fuzzy RKD Estimates

Table I of the paper reports, for local linear and local quadratic models and five bandwidth selectors, the first-stage kink (coefficient times 10510^5105) and the structural elasticity of unemployment duration with respect to benefits, with conventional standard errors and CCT robust intervals:

  • Default CCT with regularization: bandwidths of 1,460 (local linear, pilot 2,976) and 2,033 (local quadratic, pilot 3,160). The local linear first stage is −1.5-1.5−1.5 (0.6), only marginally significant (t of 2.5), with robust interval [−3.4,0.2][-3.4,0.2][−3.4,0.2]; the elasticity is 0.1 (2.4), interval [−8.4,6.0][-8.4,6.0][−8.4,6.0]. Local quadratic: first stage −3.1-3.1−3.1 (1.4), interval [−8.5,−0.7][-8.5,-0.7][−8.5,−0.7]; elasticity −2.2-2.2−2.2 (3.0), interval [−10.1,6.5][-10.1,6.5][−10.1,6.5].

  • CCT without regularization: bandwidths of 2,947 (pilot 4,898) and 5,058 (pilot 3,870). Local linear first stage −1.1-1.1−1.1 (0.2), interval [−1.4,0.2][-1.4,0.2][−1.4,0.2]; elasticity 2.7 (1.2), interval [−3.9,5.6][-3.9,5.6][−3.9,5.6]. Local quadratic first stage −0.9-0.9−0.9 (0.4), elasticity 0.1 (2.4), interval [−28.7,31.2][-28.7,31.2][−28.7,31.2].

  • Fuzzy CCT: bandwidths of 4,091 (pilot 7,162) and 3,095 (pilot 3,112). Local linear first stage −1.4-1.4−1.4 (0.1), interval [−1.8,−0.8][-1.8,-0.8][−1.8,−0.8]; elasticity 1.9 (0.6), interval [0.1,5.1][0.1,5.1][0.1,5.1], the only significant bias-corrected elasticity. Local quadratic elasticity −2.4-2.4−2.4 (7.7), interval [−34.6,47.4][-34.6,47.4][−34.6,47.4].

  • Fuzzy IK: bandwidths of 5,411 (pilot 5,210) and 4,990 (pilot 5,070). Local linear first stage −1.4-1.4−1.4 (0.1), interval [−1.7,−0.3][-1.7,-0.3][−1.7,−0.3]; elasticity 1.7 (0.4), interval [−2.0,4.6][-2.0,4.6][−2.0,4.6]. Local quadratic elasticity −0.8-0.8−0.8 (2.8).

  • FG: bandwidths of 8,959 (pilot 8,482) and 9,365 (pilot 13,276). Local linear first stage −1.5-1.5−1.5 (0.1), interval [−1.9,−0.9][-1.9,-0.9][−1.9,−0.9]; elasticity 1.4 (0.2), interval [−0.6,3.4][-0.6,3.4][−0.6,3.4]. Local quadratic first stage −1.3-1.3−1.3 (0.2), elasticity 2.1 (1.0), interval [−6.1,5.0][-6.1,5.0][−6.1,5.0].

Three conclusions emerge. First, many selectors choose small bandwidths that make both the first-stage and the structural estimates imprecise; the local linear elasticity is very unstable at small bandwidths and stabilizes between 1.4 and 1.9 for bandwidths of roughly 4,000 to 9,000 euros, the range chosen by the fuzzy CCT, fuzzy IK and FG selectors. Second, local quadratic estimators are generally very noisy, with negative point elasticities in three of five cases, and their bias-corrected first stages are insignificant in all but one case. Third, local linear bias-corrected estimates are close to the uncorrected ones, but the uncertainty about the bias correction widens the robust intervals substantially. The stable local linear estimates thus suggest an elasticity of registered unemployment duration with respect to benefits of about 1.4 to 1.9, estimated with considerable uncertainty.

References

  • Card, David, David S Lee, Zhuan Pei, and Andrea Weber. 2015. “Inference on Causal Effects in a Generalized Regression Kink Design.” Econometrica, 83(6): 2453–2483.

This is the structural outcome equation of the whole paper. YYY is the outcome (in the application, expected duration of registered unemployment in days), BBB is the continuous policy variable whose causal effect is sought (the daily UI benefit), VVV is the assignment or running variable (base-year earnings), and UUU is a vector of unobservables of any dimension mmm (ability, search costs, local labor demand, tastes for leisure). The function y(⋅)y(\cdot)y(⋅) is left completely unrestricted apart from smoothness: UUU need not enter additively, so every type uuu can have its own response ∂y(b,v,u)/∂b\partial y(b,v,u)/\partial b∂y(b,v,u)/∂b and the model allows unrestricted treatment effect heterogeneity.

Two features matter. First, VVV is allowed to enter yyy directly, so this is not an exclusion restriction: earnings may affect durations through channels other than benefits, as long as that direct effect is smooth (Assumption 2). Second, UUU may be arbitrarily correlated with VVV and hence with BBB; there is no instrument independent of UUU. The constant-effect model of equation (4) is the special case

y(b,v,u)=τb+g(v)+u,y(b,v,u)=\tau b+g(v)+u,y(b,v,u)=τb+g(v)+u,

and a proportional hazards duration model with multiplicative heterogeneity is another special case that is not additive. With a binary or duration outcome, YYY can be read as an individual probability or expected value, because the identification results only involve conditional expectations of YYY. The individual causal effect of interest is the partial derivative y1(b,v,u)y_1(b,v,u)y1​(b,v,u), which is averaged in equations (2), (6) and (18).

This defines the treatment-on-the-treated parameter for a continuous regressor (Florens, Heckman, Meghir and Vytlacil 2008), equivalent to the local average response of Altonji and Matzkin (2005). Fix a value bbb of the policy and a value vvv of the running variable. Among all units that actually have B=bB=bB=b and V=vV=vV=v, the unobservables UUU follow the conditional distribution FU∣B=b,V=vF_{U|B=b,V=v}FU∣B=b,V=v​. The parameter averages each unit's marginal effect ∂y(b,v,u)/∂b\partial y(b,v,u)/\partial b∂y(b,v,u)/∂b (units: days of unemployment per euro of daily benefit) over exactly that distribution.

The word "treated" refers to the fact that the averaging is over the types who are observed at (b,v)(b,v)(b,v), not over the whole population. In a constant-effect model all marginal effects equal τ\tauτ and TTb∣v=τTT_{b|v}=\tauTTb∣v​=τ. With heterogeneity, TTb∣vTT_{b|v}TTb∣v​ answers the question: if every unit currently at (b,v)(b,v)(b,v) got a slightly larger benefit, by how much would their average outcome change?

In the sharp RK design B=b(V)B=b(V)B=b(V) is a function of VVV, so the event {B=b(0),V=0}\{B=b(0),V=0\}{B=b(0),V=0} coincides with {V=0}\{V=0\}{V=0} and the relevant distribution is simply FU∣V=0F_{U|V=0}FU∣V=0​. Equation (6) shows that this is precisely the parameter identified at the kink, with (b,v)=(b0,0)(b,v)=(b_0,0)(b,v)=(b0​,0), and equation (12) relates it to the version TTbTT_bTTb​ that does not condition on VVV.

This is the motivating policy rule: unemployment insurance pays a fixed replacement rate ρ\rhoρ of previous earnings VVV until earnings reach the threshold TTT, after which the benefit is capped at the maximum ρT\rho TρT. In Austria ρ\rhoρ is 0.55 of net daily earnings. The rule is continuous everywhere but kinked at V=TV=TV=T:

b′(v)={ρ,v<T0,v>T,lim⁡v→T+b′(v)−lim⁡v→T−b′(v)=−ρ.b'(v)=\begin{cases}\rho, & v<T\\ 0, & v>T\end{cases},\qquad \lim_{v\to T^+}b'(v)-\lim_{v\to T^-}b'(v)=-\rho.b′(v)={ρ,0,​v<Tv>T​,v→T+lim​b′(v)−v→T−lim​b′(v)=−ρ.

Because BBB is a deterministic function of VVV, there is no variation in BBB holding VVV fixed, and any variable independent of VVV is also independent of BBB, so neither conventional IV nor nonparametric regression on (B,V)(B,V)(B,V) can separate the effect of BBB from that of VVV. The RK idea is that a causal effect of BBB should transmit the kink in b(⋅)b(\cdot)b(⋅) to a kink in E[Y∣V=v]E[Y|V=v]E[Y∣V=v] at the same point, while the direct effect of VVV and the composition of types change smoothly there. After normalizing T=0T=0T=0 (recentering earnings at each year's threshold), b0=b(0)b_0=b(0)b0​=b(0) is the maximum benefit, and the denominator of equations (5) and (25) equals −ρ-\rho−ρ. Continuity of the rule (no jump in level) is what Assumption 3 requires; Remark 3 and equation (13) treat the case of a jump.

This is the constant-effect additive model used by Nielsen, Sorensen and Taber (2010) to justify the RKD. The coefficient τ\tauτ is a single causal effect of BBB on YYY shared by every unit; g(V)g(V)g(V) is an arbitrary function capturing the direct effect of the running variable (for example, higher earners may search differently regardless of benefits); and ε\varepsilonε is an additive error that may be correlated with VVV, so E[ε∣V=v]E[\varepsilon|V=v]E[ε∣V=v] need not be zero or constant.

Additivity and homogeneity are strong. They imply that all units respond identically and that unobservables only shift the level of YYY. They rule out, for example, a proportional hazards model where the benefit coefficient multiplies an individual baseline hazard, or any setting in which the response to benefits varies with unobserved characteristics. The model is the special case y(b,v,u)=τb+g(v)+uy(b,v,u)=\tau b+g(v)+uy(b,v,u)=τb+g(v)+u of equation (1) with U=εU=\varepsilonU=ε.

Identification requires only that ggg and E[ε∣V=v]E[\varepsilon|V=v]E[ε∣V=v] be continuously differentiable at v=0v=0v=0; then the only source of a slope change in E[Y∣V=v]E[Y|V=v]E[Y∣V=v] is τ\tauτ times the slope change of bbb, which gives equation (5). The paper's contribution is to show that the same estimand remains interpretable, as a weighted average of heterogeneous marginal effects, in the nonseparable model of equation (1).

This specifies measurement error in both the assignment variable and the policy. VVV and BBB are the true values; the econometrician sees V∗V^*V∗ and B∗B^*B∗. Each error is the product of a binary indicator and a continuous component: UV=GV⋅UV′U_V=G_V\cdot U_{V'}UV​=GV​⋅UV′​ equals the continuous error UV′U_{V'}UV′​ when GV=1G_V=1GV​=1 and is exactly zero when GV=0G_V=0GV​=0, and similarly for UBU_BUB​. Hence the error distribution is a mixture of a point mass at zero and a continuous distribution.

The continuous components (UV′,UB′)(U_{V'},U_{B'})(UV′​,UB′​) have a joint density, conditional on (U,ε)(U,\varepsilon)(U,ε), on a compact rectangle; they may be correlated with each other, with VVV (Assumption 4a) and with the unobservables. This is much more general than classical measurement error.

Why the mixture? A unit with GV=1G_V=1GV​=1 has its observed running variable V∗=V+UV′V^*=V+U_{V'}V∗=V+UV′​ smeared by a continuous error, so the kink of its own schedule at V=0V=0V=0 is spread over a range of V∗V^*V∗ and leaves no kink in E[B∗∣V∗]E[B^*|V^*]E[B∗∣V∗] or E[Y∣V∗]E[Y|V^*]E[Y∣V∗] at v∗=0v^*=0v∗=0 (see the derivation of equation (18)). Only the point mass GV=0G_V=0GV​=0 preserves a sharp kink in the data. This is why Assumption 3a (equation (17)) requires Pr⁡[UV=0∣⋅]>0\Pr[U_V=0|\cdot]>0Pr[UV​=0∣⋅]>0 for a nonnegligible group. No point mass is needed for UBU_BUB​, since additive noise in B∗B^*B∗ that is smooth in VVV only adds a smooth term to the first stage. In the Austrian data most claims lie exactly on the statutory schedule, interpreted as a mass point at zero.

These are the four probabilities, for i,j∈{0,1}i,j\in\{0,1\}i,j∈{0,1}, of the joint pattern of measurement-error indicators: π00\pi^{00}π00 is the probability that both VVV and BBB are measured exactly, π10\pi^{10}π10 that only VVV is mismeasured, π01\pi^{01}π01 that only BBB is mismeasured, and π11\pi^{11}π11 that both are. They sum to one. Conditioning on (V,U,ε,UV′,UB′)(V,U,\varepsilon,U_{V'},U_{B'})(V,U,ε,UV′​,UB′​) means the chance of an error may depend on the true earnings, on the type, on the compliance or dependents status, and even on the size of the latent errors, so the errors are not assumed to be missing at random.

The probability that the running variable is correctly measured, which appears in the weights of equation (19), is obtained by integrating out the continuous components:

Pr⁡[UV=0∣V=v,U=u,ε=e]=E[π00+π01 ∣ V=v,U=u,ε=e],\Pr[U_V=0|V=v,U=u,\varepsilon=e]=E\left[\pi^{00}+\pi^{01}\,\big|\,V=v,U=u,\varepsilon=e\right],Pr[UV​=0∣V=v,U=u,ε=e]=E[π00+π01​V=v,U=u,ε=e],

using that UV′U_{V'}UV′​ is continuous so UV′=0U_{V'}=0UV′​=0 has probability zero. Assumption 5 requires each πij\pi^{ij}πij and its derivative in vvv to be continuous. Combined with Assumption 4a, this makes the share of correctly measured units evolve smoothly through V=0V=0V=0; otherwise a kink in the probability of misreporting earnings at the threshold would create a spurious kink in the observed first stage and reduced form, and would also show up as a kink in fV∗f_{V^*}fV∗​ (Corollary 1).

These are the individual one-sided slopes of the fuzzy policy rule at the threshold. In the UI illustration, a claimant who follows the no-dependents schedule has slope ρ\rhoρ below and 000 above the threshold, so the individual kink is −ρ-\rho−ρ. Because family supplements are added without a cap and the schedules for different numbers of dependents are parallel, every type has the same kink −ρ-\rho−ρ at the same point, which is why monotonicity (Assumption 6) holds in the application. A type whose schedule is not kinked at 000 (for instance a schedule with a different threshold) has b1+(e)=b1−(e)b_1^+(e)=b_1^-(e)b1+​(e)=b1−​(e) and receives zero weight in equation (19). Note that b1(⋅)b_1(\cdot)b1​(⋅) and b0(⋅)b_0(\cdot)b0​(⋅) in the UI illustration of the note denote the schedules with and without dependents, a different use of the subscript from the derivative b1(v,e)b_1(v,e)b1​(v,e) here. This is the fuzzy first-stage condition of Assumption 3a, requiring a nonnegligible population at the kink. The integral runs over the policy types eee in AεA_\varepsilonAε​, those with positive density of VVV at the threshold. For each such type it multiplies three factors: the probability that the running variable of a type-eee unit at V=0V=0V=0 is measured without error, Pr⁡[UV=0∣V=0,ε=e]\Pr[U_V=0|V=0,\varepsilon=e]Pr[UV​=0∣V=0,ε=e]; the absolute size of that type's kink, ∣b1+(e)−b1−(e)∣|b_1^+(e)-b_1^-(e)|∣b1+​(e)−b1−​(e)∣ from equation (16); and the density fV∣ε=e(0)f_{V|\varepsilon=e}(0)fV∣ε=e​(0) of being at the threshold. The integral is positive only if a set of types of positive probability simultaneously has a real kink, is correctly measured with positive probability, and has positive density at 000.

Each factor corresponds to a channel that can destroy the first stage. If nobody's schedule is kinked, there is nothing to exploit. If every observation is smeared by continuous error, the kink in E[B∗∣V∗]E[B^*|V^*]E[B∗∣V∗] disappears (equation (14)). If nobody is near the threshold, the kink is uninformative. Up to the positive factor fV(0)f_V(0)fV​(0), the integral is the absolute value of the denominator of equation (19) when monotonicity holds, so Assumption 3a together with Assumption 6 guarantees a nonzero first-stage kink. Conversely, finding a significant kink in E[B∗∣V∗=v∗]E[B^*|V^*=v^*]E[B∗∣V∗=v∗] at 000 is evidence for these assumptions (Remark 4). The absolute value is used because the assumption is stated before imposing monotonicity.

This is the binary-treatment extension (Remark 6). The outcome depends on a binary treatment TTT (college attendance), the running variable VVV (parental income) and unobservables UUU; the continuous variable BBB (financial aid) does not enter yyy, which is the exclusion restriction. Treatment is chosen by a threshold-crossing rule: T=1T=1T=1 when the latent index T∗=t(B,V,η)T^*=t(B,V,\eta)T∗=t(B,V,η) is nonnegative, with η\etaη a scalar error (taste for college) that may be correlated with UUU. These are the two one-sided local polynomial regressions of the outcome on the running variable used to estimate the reduced-form slopes. The superscripts −-− and +++ refer to the n−n^-n− observations with V<0V<0V<0 and the n+n^+n+ observations with V≥0V\geq0V≥0 (running variable recentred at the threshold). On each side one fits a polynomial of order ppp in VVV by weighted least squares, with kernel weights K(Vi/h)K(V_i/h)K(Vi​/h) that are zero outside the bandwidth hhh (uniform kernel: equal weight inside [−h,h][-h,h][−h,h]). The coefficients β~j±\tilde{\beta}^\pm_jβ~​j±​ are the choice variables; the solutions are β^j±\hat{\beta}^\pm_jβ^​j±​.

The coefficient of interest is the linear term: since a polynomial expansion of E[Y∣V=v]E[Y|V=v]E[Y∣V=v] around 000 has first-order coefficient equal to the derivative,

β^1+≈lim⁡v→0+dE[Y∣V=v]dv,β^1−≈lim⁡v→0−dE[Y∣V=v]dv.\hat{\beta}^+_1\approx\lim_{v\to0^+}\frac{dE[Y|V=v]}{dv},\qquad\hat{\beta}^-_1\approx\lim_{v\to0^-}\frac{dE[Y|V=v]}{dv}.β^​1+​≈v→0+lim​dvdE[Y∣V=v]​,β^​1−​≈v→0−lim​dvdE[Y∣V=v]​.

Separate fits on each side are needed because the slope is allowed to differ at the threshold; fitting a single polynomial would smooth over the kink. Local linear (p=1p=1p=1) or local quadratic (p=2p=2p=2) fits are used. The bandwidth trades off bias from curvature in E[Y∣V]E[Y|V]E[Y∣V] against variance, and the polynomial order trades off bias order against noise (equation (28)). These slopes form the numerators of equations (25) and (27).

This is the sharp RKD estimator, the sample analog of equation (5) and of the left-hand side of equation (6). The numerator is the estimated change in the slope of the outcome at the threshold, from the local polynomial fits of equation (24). The denominator is the change in the slope of the policy rule, which is known exactly in a sharp design: κ1+=lim⁡v→0+b′(v)\kappa^+_1=\lim_{v\to0^+}b'(v)κ1+​=limv→0+​b′(v) and κ1−=lim⁡v→0−b′(v)\kappa^-_1=\lim_{v\to0^-}b'(v)κ1−​=limv→0−​b′(v). Because the denominator is a constant, all sampling variability comes from the numerator, and the estimator inherits its rate (equation (28)).

In the UI rule of equation (3), κ1−=ρ\kappa^-_1=\rhoκ1−​=ρ and κ1+=0\kappa^+_1=0κ1+​=0, so the denominator is −ρ-\rho−ρ. A flattening of the duration profile above the threshold, β^1+<β^1−\hat{\beta}^+_1<\hat{\beta}^-_1β^​1+​<β^​1−​, therefore implies a positive effect of benefits on durations:

τ^SRKD=β^1+−β^1−−ρ>0whenβ^1+<β^1−.\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{SRKD}}=\frac{\hat{\beta}^+_1-\hat{\beta}^-_1}{-\rho}>0\quad\text{when}\quad\hat{\beta}^+_1<\hat{\beta}^-_1.τ^SRKD​=−ρβ^​1+​−β^​1−​​>0whenβ^​1+​<β^​1−​.

The estimate is in units of outcome per unit of policy (days per euro of daily benefit); the paper reports elasticities, which rescale it by the ratio of benefit to duration at the threshold. Its interpretation is the TT parameter at the kink, a weighted average of marginal effects with the weights of equation (6).

These are the first-stage local polynomial regressions in a fuzzy design. They are identical to equation (24) except that the dependent variable is the observed policy BiB_iBi​ (daily benefit) instead of YiY_iYi​; as in the paper, asterisks on B∗B^*B∗ and V∗V^*V∗ are dropped, so BBB and VVV here are the observed, possibly mismeasured, values. The same kernel KKK, bandwidth hhh and order ppp are used on each side, and the linear coefficients estimate the one-sided slopes of the observed first stage:

κ^1±≈lim⁡v∗→0±dE[B∗∣V∗=v∗]dv∗.\hat{\kappa}^\pm_1\approx\lim_{v^*\to0^\pm}\frac{dE[B^*|V^*=v^*]}{dv^*}.κ^1±​≈v∗→0±lim​dv∗dE[B∗∣V∗=v∗]​.

In a fuzzy design these slopes are unknown, because the statutory schedule is only followed by part of the sample: dependents' supplements, noncompliance and measurement error make E[B∗∣V∗]E[B^*|V^*]E[B∗∣V∗] a blurred version of the statutory rule. In the Austrian data the observed benefit profile still has a positive slope above the threshold, because the average number of dependents, and hence family allowances, rises with earnings; this does not matter, since only the change in slope enters. A significant first-stage kink is also a test of Assumptions 3a and 6 (Remark 4). Using the same hhh in both regressions keeps the ratio in equation (27) a Wald-type estimator on a common sample.

This is the fuzzy RKD estimator, the sample analog of the left-hand side of equation (18). Numerator and denominator are the estimated slope changes of the reduced form (equation (24)) and of the observed first stage (equation (26)). It is the kink analog of the fuzzy RD, or Wald, estimator: in a fuzzy RD one divides the jump in E[Y∣V]E[Y|V]E[Y∣V] by the jump in the treatment probability; here one divides the change in slope of E[Y∣V∗]E[Y|V^*]E[Y∣V∗] by the change in slope of E[B∗∣V∗]E[B^*|V^*]E[B∗∣V∗]. Equivalently, it is the IV estimate in which the interaction of the running variable with an above-threshold indicator instruments for BBB, controlling for a separate intercept above the threshold and the remaining polynomial terms on each side (an exactly identified IV regression, whose coefficient is the ratio of the reduced-form to the first-stage coefficient).

By Proposition 2, the probability limit (as h→0h\to0h→0) is a weighted average of marginal effects y1(b(0,e),0,u)y_1(b(0,e),0,u)y1​(b(0,e),0,u) with the nonnegative weights φ(u,e)\varphi(u,e)φ(u,e) of equation (19). Because the denominator is estimated, the estimator behaves like a ratio: when the first-stage kink is small relative to its standard error, the ratio is unstable and conventional inference is unreliable, as with weak instruments. This is visible in the application, where small bandwidths give imprecise first stages and very unstable elasticities, and the estimates stabilize at 1.4 to 1.9 only for bandwidths of roughly 4,000 to 9,000 euros. The delta method gives its asymptotic variance (equation (28)).

These are the asymptotic distributions of the sharp and fuzzy RKD estimators of polynomial order ppp, taken from Lemmas A1 and A2 of Calonico, Cattaneo and Titiunik (2014). The symbol ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ denotes convergence in distribution, ϱ\varrhoϱ is the leading bias constant and Ω\OmegaΩ the asymptotic variance.

The rate comes from estimating a derivative at a boundary. About nhnhnh observations fall in the window, so a level is estimated with standard deviation of order 1/nh1/\sqrt{nh}1/nh​ (the RD rate); a slope is a level difference divided by a distance of order hhh, giving

s.d.(β^1)∝1hnh=1nh3.\text{s.d.}\left(\hat{\beta}_1\right)\propto\frac{1}{h\sqrt{nh}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{nh^3}}.s.d.(β^​1​)∝hnh​1​=nh3​1​.

The bias: an order-ppp polynomial leaves a remainder of order hp+1h^{p+1}hp+1 in levels, which becomes hph^php for the first derivative, hence the centering term hpϱh^p\varrhohpϱ. Balancing squared bias h2ph^{2p}h2p against variance 1/(nh3)1/(nh^3)1/(nh3) gives the MSE-optimal bandwidth h∝n−1/(2p+3)h\propto n^{-1/(2p+3)}h∝n−1/(2p+3). At that bandwidth nh3 hp\sqrt{nh^3}\,h^pnh3​hp converges to a nonzero constant, so the bias does not vanish relative to the standard error, which is the reason for the bias correction in equation (29). The fuzzy variance ΩFRKD,p\Omega_{\mathrm{FRKD},p}ΩFRKD,p​ follows from the delta method applied to the ratio in equation (27), and grows as the first-stage kink shrinks. Imposing continuity of E[Y∣V]E[Y|V]E[Y∣V] in estimation leaves Ω\OmegaΩ and ϱ\varrhoϱ unchanged with a uniform kernel.

This is the robust bias-corrected inference procedure of Calonico, Cattaneo and Titiunik (2014). The first expression subtracts an estimate of the leading bias from equation (28): ϱ^p\hat{\varrho}_pϱ^​p​ is obtained from a local polynomial of higher order q≥p+1q\geq p+1q≥p+1 with a pilot bandwidth hqh_qhq​, which estimates the higher derivatives that drive the bias, and it is multiplied by hph^php. The second expression is the 95 percent confidence interval centered at the corrected estimate.

The key innovation is the variance varpbc\mathrm{var}^{bc}_pvarpbc​. A naive bias correction would use the variance of τ^p\hat{\tau}_pτ^p​ alone and treat the bias estimate as known. Here the variance accounts for the sampling noise of both τ^p\hat{\tau}_pτ^p​ and hpϱ^ph^p\hat{\varrho}_phpϱ^​p​, and their covariance, since both are computed from overlapping data. This yields intervals that are wider but have correct coverage even at the MSE-optimal bandwidth, where conventional intervals undercover. The validity of the variance formula requires that the pilot and main bandwidths shrink at the same rate, hq/h→ρ∈(0,∞)h_q/h\to\rho\in(0,\infty)hq​/h→ρ∈(0,∞); this ρ\rhoρ is a bandwidth ratio, unrelated to the replacement rate ρ\rhoρ of equation (3).

In the application the cost of robustness is clear: local linear bias-corrected point estimates are close to the uncorrected ones, but the robust intervals are much wider. For example, with the fuzzy CCT bandwidth the elasticity is 1.9 with robust interval [0.1,5.1][0.1,5.1][0.1,5.1], the only significant one among the stable estimates.
